en: Giving it up entirely,
Standing for honor,
Fighting without wavering,
A tremendous fight took place.
Mighty Bilgich grew angry,
We are ninety-four; these are two,
Your vigor exhausted and strength fled,
Has our strength really gone?
All of you swarm them and fight!
Let calamity be brought about,
See what fate has written upon your heads,
Does anyone return from death?
Can a man with a belt at his waist
Ever return from death?
Gathering courage and shouting,
The black scourge, Chong Bilgich,
Those left after the dead,
He drove in, sweeping them onward.
Trampling the battlefield,
Berating all the champions,
Making the spearmen rush,
The mad brute thundered,
Making the wide world narrow,
Showing his hellish aspect,
Making his mountainlike courage firm,
Working mysteries unknown to men,
His wisdom, cunning, and strength,
Making them stronger than the world,
Bringing twilight and binding sight,
Toppling mountains and conjuring weather,
Raising turmoil equal to hell,
Caught by the wrathful one,
The times narrowed and broke down,
The earth grew misty with dust,
Hills, cliffs, and great mountains,
Snow hid the stones from sight,
The weather worsened into winter,
He cast a fierce weather spell,
Do not ask about Chong Bilgich,
Skillful on horseback and swift on foot,
Dexterous with a spear and exceedingly adept,
Knowing its techniques, exceedingly accomplished,
His father was the hunter Kojojash,
Watching his stratagems,
If your means fail, flee back,
His onslaught became deep-rooted strength,
No living soul withstood his bow,
His menace and venom,
No creature could endure,
The earth darkened and the water surged,
A full-fledged battle took place,
Riding matched gray horses,
Wearing an ample, excellent coat,
The heroes Seytek and Ak Joltoy,
Their protecting power
Bore these men aloft.
The spirits of their forefathers
Bore them greatly aloft.
Untroubled, scarcely blinking,
That wrath of Chong Bilgich
The fierce hero endured unconcerned,
Fighting in turns,
Against Chong Bilgich's wrath,
Against the venom he unleashed,
Standing without submitting,
Unfathomable Ak Joltoy
Saddled Kulansur.
Of the spells known to humankind,
He recited every one.
The great sorcerer Chong Bilgich
Sent a biting wind blowing,
Making it mottled blue and breaking it apart,
Making all the fog unravel,
Ak Joltoy proved a champion,
Making God's sun appear,
The hell of the piercing wind
Ak Joltoy kept suppressing,
God's sun, brilliantly bright,
Ak Joltoy kept revealing.
Chong Bilgich, no longer raging,
Had come into the sunlight,
Bilgich, no longer raising hell,
Had begun to speak.
When we left Great Kakan,
We were a chosen hundred,
The hundred died; I remained,
Look, Joltoy, toward Kakan,

en: Still bore the fault of innocence.
He pursued the cunning fugitive:
Black without and cold within,
He chased the sorcerer, saying,
“If I do not turn Kulunsur’s head,
If I do not pursue this maddened Bilgich
All the way to Beijing itself!”
“If I do not shatter his throne and game,
If I do not slaughter this hulking slave,
If I do not hew clean through his neck,
If I do not catch, devour, and butcher him,
May I sink into darkness as though never born!
They used to say that the foe who flees
Will take for his wife
The finest of black-haired beauties,
The best among all women.
But I shall spill his blood at last;
I shall seize him by the trailing hem,
And cast that accursed, doomed Bilgich
To be torn apart in the gray-wolf game.
The people will clamor in uproar,
And despair of their wrathful champion;
They will say, ‘He was born of a noble man,’
And my lineage will become known.
All forty khanates of China
Will understand and despair of life!”
So spoke brave Seytek,
Consumed by fierce intent,
Brandishing and driving with his spear.
His eyes fixed on great Bilgich,
He followed directly behind,
While the black earth, though not split in two,
Endured the pounding through its depths.
Every rise was gouged away;
Wherever the hooves struck squarely,
Trenches were carved like canals.
It became tumult, calamity, and strife,
A terror no living soul could bear.
When they entered the downward slope,
Brave Bilgich’s great Kerik
Stretched his forelegs like a deer;
When they began climbing uphill,
Kulunsur swept on like a whirlwind—
Such was the ground of their pursuit.
Amid this tale of endless tumult,
They had now drawn close
To the place established as an ambush,
Where Bilgich’s army lay concealed.
Unable to bear his wounds,
Yet still the warrior Akjoltoy
Had ridden after Seytek.
Upon the matchless Kulunsur,
He whipped him right and left,
Spurred him on from either side,
And shouted in anger,
Calling out to Khan Seytek.
Kulunsur, whom no living creature could catch,
Shot whirring like an arrow;
When he passed over black stones,
They burst apart like charcoal.
Ah, wondrous beast Kulunsur,
He flew rumbling like a cloud,
His tail streaming over his haunches,
His matchless breeding plain to see.
From the black mountains of Kaspang,
From the mouth of Kapka-Tash,
From the heights of Dyngsha,
From the fortress no mortal had entered,
The stronghold firmly sealed,
Uncle Joltoy caught up
At the ridge of the Sentry Stone.
He tugged at his armor,
Shaking him about the head and eyes:
“You have courage but no sense;
You are a witless Seytek!
By refusing to heed advice,
Will you send Joltoy to the grave?
To a place where no man can pass,
Will you cast us upon the embers?
Without even binding our hands and feet,
Will you cast us into the fire?
Alas, Seytek, may ruin take you—
My child, what if the two of us are parted?
Did I not tell you before
That the accursed Khagan
Has paths narrower than a hair
And passes even I cannot cross?
“In Beijing, where wrath cannot penetrate,
His people swarm like black beetles.
This is the great nation of China,
A place where men settle only for battle,
Where your first forefather led the charge
And the land sucked dry all who fought.
There, parted from his lions,
Your first forefather met his end.
It is no cheap land like an open ridge,
Nor is Bilgich a common warrior.
If we go any farther,
There are iron-walled enclosures
And deeply excavated pits.
There are armies of that madman,
So dense the sun cannot be seen.
Anyone who falls in cannot leap back out;
Their stubborn traps are hell itself.
That senseless scourge
Commands a well-arrayed host of ten thousand.
Once locked in combat, they never retreat;
It is a radiant and exalted land,
Where the people of Chin-Machin dwell.
Their warriors butcher any who provoke them;
They are a people who ask, ‘Where is strife?’
Whenever one among them dies,
They roast and eat another.
When their giant rage possesses them,
They strike down and eat any crow they see,
And surround and devour any wild ass.
They flare up anew whenever diminished;
No living being has ever reached their root.
Though slaughter lasts for years,
Their baleful power never fades,
No wrathful enemy could prevail against this

en: Such was the state of great Bilgich.
When Bilgich appeared like this,
They had the great doors shut,
And slaughtered eighty black bulls
As sacrificial offerings.
Red-gowned and slender-waisted,
Beautiful women with dainty feet—
For women’s hands were said to bring relief—
Were set to tend him.
They shouted for the skilled healers
And summoned all the physicians.
The physicians of China,
Those who diagnosed by feeling the pulse,
The most accomplished masters of medicine,
Their experts standing forty rows deep—
Now the great physicians examined him.
“Alas, this Burut foe is formidable!
How many men among us
Have been ruined by him?” they said.
The great lungs that drew his breath
“It turned out badly,” he said,
The physician was skillful,
From his wound, with a great probe,
They sucked it all out together.
In the populous realm of China
There are medicines for every need,
Every kind of remedy is there.
They gave him powdered red medicine
To take internally.
The pain of the wound subsided,
His closed eyes opened,
Chongbilgich returned to the light.
When seven days had passed,
Chongbilgich regained his speech,
And slowly began to speak with force,
Addressing his sovereign Kite,
He began these words:
“We were a hundred champions skilled in sorcery,
We broke through their defenses and opened a path,
We attacked that aroused nation.
We saw might surpassing all the world,
We saw great torments like those of hell.
We gathered up the riches,
But all ninety-nine companions
Were slaughtered in a yawning pit.
Chongbilgich alone remained,
I despaired of my precious life;
My prowess did not save me from death,
Never have I seen calamity like this.
I have no commander, no people,
No champion remains to shelter me.
The two giants Akjoltoy and Seytek
Caught me between them,
Yet I escaped their swift steeds,
And turned back after assailing the Buruts.
I went there boasting of valor,
But was parted from my champions,
It cools, softly murmuring,

en: “He truly is Teñir,” they said,
While old and young cried out in amazement.
Blessed by Kyzyr, he gained strength,
Seized the whole Chinese nation,
Drove them into a single hollow,
And packed them into a single pit.
When anyone died, he had the corpse
Cast into the fire and burned,
Enforcing his supreme decree.
Over the vast Chinese realm
And the many Kalmyk and Shibe peoples,
He became an absolute khan;
Whoever opposed him was slaughtered.
He was mounted upon the horse called Chyngteñir,
And Teñir remained to rule the nation.
Let us leave this tale here,
His founding ancestor was Nogoy Khan,

en: Was born the hero Seytek.
He reached Talas safely,
Recovered the scattered herds,
Wrestled with his foes and took the khanate,
Then returned once more to Talas.
He became a man of weight,
A majestic khan,
Making the broad-backed Ala-Too
A settled and ordered homeland.
The ancestral realm left by his father
He tended wholly and made into a nation.
He turned every weakling into a man of substance,
And gave the homeless a homeland;
He made all his people skilled.
When weary, he had gazelles hunted,
And let the people live and play in ease.
While Seytek watched over them,
The people’s hearts were at peace,
And they became immensely wealthy.
He achieved all that he intended,
And filled every chest
With yellow gold and treasure.
They dressed in fox and sable,
And lived as though in the blessed Night of Power.
His people, countless in number, grew rich,
And the nation’s heart was at peace.
As they sat governing the people,
The leopards Seytek and Akjoltoy
Together served as ruling khans.
Such was the state of their people:
No outsider dared travel among them,
And none who attacked remained alive.
They stood like the barrier of Mount Kap,
Lions guarding their nation;
Thus did those noble men live.
Then, when the people began moving uphill,
At the season when horses’ coats turn dark,
When the grass had reached full growth,
The people headed for the summer pastures
And settled on the lower slopes;
The nation spread out and made camp.
The noble lady Bermet,
The renowned wife of Seytek,
Craved tiger meat in her pregnancy.
Her craving drove her to agitation,
For a wondrous child was within her,
And she could scarcely bear its force.
Learning of this, Akjoltoy
Struck down a bear far away.
For six days and then seven,
He was gone upon the hunt.

en: Your uncle Akjoltay.
With uncommon foresight he made his plan;
Turning toward his right,
Without letting anyone know,
Without alerting a single soul,
He leaned aside,
Filled out his robe,
Slipped his hand into his pouch,
And drew out a fist-sized object.
Disregard it and shame will follow:
“My steadfast child Akbermet,
This pale walnut, large as a fist,
The holy wanderer Khizr
Has entrusted to you.
Eat it, my little one;
Your grime-covered heart will open,
And your frenzy will subside.
My child Bermet, heed me:
I have become your healer.
May you be mother of the nation
That bears a lionhearted champion.
Accept your trust, my child,
Purest among women in flowing skirts,
Foremost among women in white kerchiefs.
Eat it, and it will quench your thirst;
